chunks: PCB manufacturing and assembly flow. The question: Describe the PCB manufacturing and assembly process.
Building a finished board happens on an assembly line, one station after another.
Solder paste is printed on the pads (the copper spots where parts are soldered), machines place the parts, an oven melts the solder, and cameras and testers check the result.
Each station has a job, and the line is set up so a defect is caught as early as possible, when it is cheap to fix.
Think of making pizzas in a busy kitchen. One person spreads the sauce, another sets the toppings, the oven bakes them, and someone checks each pizza before it leaves.
A missing topping is cheap to fix at the topping station and costly once the pizza is boxed and delivered. The line also moves only as fast as its slowest station.
Unlike pizza, a board may go through twice, once for each side.
Time runs top to bottom. Early stations (print, SPI) are cheap places to find defects; late stations (functional test) find the most but cost the most to diagnose.
For a double-sided board, the print-to-AOI steps repeat for the second side before the through-hole step.
Solder paste: tiny solder balls mixed with a sticky cleaning agent called flux, printed through a metal stencil onto the pads.
Surface-mount (SMT): parts that sit flat on pads instead of having legs through holes. Pick-and-place: the machine that sets parts onto the paste.
Reflow: the oven step that melts the paste into solder joints. Through-hole parts: parts with legs pushed through holes, soldered in a separate step.
Inspection and test: camera checks and electrical checks that find bad boards.
Say a board has 400 parts, and the placement machine sets 20,000 parts per hour. That is 3600 / 20,000 = 0. 18 seconds per part, so 400 parts take 72 seconds.
If printing takes 25 seconds and the oven passes a board every 60 seconds, the placement machine is the slowest station.
It sets the pace of the whole line: 3600 / 72 = 50 boards per hour. That is the whole idea.

"A typical SMT line prints solder paste through a stencil, inspects the paste, places components with a pick-and-place machine, then sends the board through a reflow oven that melts the paste into joints, followed by AOI.

Double-sided boards are flipped and repeated, through-hole parts are soldered by wave, selective or hand soldering, and then the board goes through in-circuit or flying-probe test and a functional test, plus coating and depaneling.
The idea is to catch defects as early as possible."
